---
title: Getting started
---

In this tutorial you set up a Python project, read results from a MIKE 21 flow model of the Øresund, plot them, and save the maximum water level to a new dfsu file.

MIKE IO runs on Windows and Linux. On Windows it needs the [VC++ redistributables](https://aka.ms/vs/17/release/vc_redist.x64.exe), which are already installed if you have MIKE.

## Set up a project

Install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/). uv installs Python for you, so you don't need a Python installation first.

Create a project folder with MIKE IO and JupyterLab in it:

```bash
uv init mikeio-tutorial
cd mikeio-tutorial
uv add mikeio jupyterlab
```

Download [oresundHD_run1.dfsu](https://github.com/DHI/mikeio/raw/main/tests/testdata/oresundHD_run1.dfsu) into the `mikeio-tutorial` folder, then start JupyterLab:

```bash
uv run jupyter lab
```

Create a new notebook and type the code below into its cells.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import shutil

shutil.copy("../data/oresundHD_run1.dfsu", ".");
```

## Read the file

```{python}
import mikeio

ds = mikeio.read("oresundHD_run1.dfsu")
ds
```

`ds` is a [Dataset](dataset.qmd). The summary shows that the file holds four items on a mesh of 3612 elements, with one value per day from 7 to 11 March 2018.

## Pick out one item

```{python}
da = ds["Surface elevation"]
da
```

`da` is a [DataArray](dataarray.qmd): the values of one item, together with its time axis and mesh.

Plot the surface elevation on the last day:

```{python}
da.sel(time="2018-03-11").plot();
```

## Look at one location

Select the element that contains a point, given in the coordinates of the mesh (UTM zone 33):

```{python}
point = da.sel(x=355000, y=6160000)
point
```

The result is a time series. Plot it:

```{python}
point.plot();
```

## Save the maximum water level

Take the maximum over time in each element:

```{python}
max_elevation = da.max(axis="time")
max_elevation.plot(title="Maximum surface elevation");
```

Write it to a new dfsu file:

```{python}
max_elevation.to_dfs("max_elevation.dfsu")
```

Read it back to check the result:

```{python}
mikeio.read("max_elevation.dfsu")
```

You can open `max_elevation.dfsu` in MIKE Zero like any other dfsu file.
